newsitem.title: USA: Witness denies Clinton link in Hubbel contract.
newsitem.headline: Witness denies Clinton link in Hubbel contract.

text.p: Neither President Clinton nor his wife Hillary intervened to win a consulting contract for disgraced former associate Webster Hubbell, a witness told the Whitewater grand jury Thursday.

"Absolutely not. There was never a mention to us by anyone in the administration or that it should be done for someone in the administration," said Ted Stein, a former chairman of the Los Angeles, California, Airport Commission.

Stein spoke with reporters after appearing before the grand jury during which he said he was asked if White House officials, including the Clintons, had played a role in winning a consulting contract for Webster Hubbell, a former assistant attorney general. He was convicted of stealing money from the Little Rock law firm where he and Hillary Clinton were once partners.
Stein said prosecutors asked him "a series of questions" about whether the Clintons had influenced the hiring of Hubbell "and the answer to all those questions was negative."
Hubbell was hired by the Los Angeles Airport Commission in 1994 to lobby the federal Transportation Department in a dispute over airport revenues.
He was paid $24,750 and was to collect a similar sum, but he was fired upon entering a guilty plea to theft and fraud charges brought by the Whitewater special prosecutor in December 1994.
Stein said Hubbell had described his problems with the Rose Law Firm, where he and Mrs. Clinton had been partners, as "strictly a billing dispute."
Stein said Hubbell was referred to the Airport Commission by Mary E. Leslie and her husband, Alan S. Arkatov. Both are Democrats who have worked actively on Clinton's behalf.

Stein noted that both Leslie and Arkatov were working for the re-election of Los Angeles city attorney James Hahn, whom Stein sought to unseat. Stein suggested his appearance before the grand jury was disclosed in a bid to embarrass him.

White House critics suggested the Los Angeles contract and other legal work was obtained for Hubbell in exchange for his silence on the Clintons' alleged involvement in matters under the scrutiny of Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr.
In an unrelated development, Clinton's partner in the Whitewater real estate project, James McDougal, was granted a second delay in sentencing on Thursday.

In papers filed in federal court in Little Rock, Starr requested the postponement in order to evaluate information provided by McDougal, who cooperated with Starr after his 1996 conviction for fraud and conspiracy.

"I don't think a prudent person would speculate on where this case is or how much time it might consume," said McDougal, reached at his Arkadelphia, Arkansas, home. "It seems to me it's already taken up a lifetime."
McDougal's sentencing was rescheduled from late February to April.

McDougal and his former wife, Susan, were convicted in the first jury trial brought by the Whitewater prosecutors, who are investigating the personal and political finances of President and Mrs. Clinton. Convicted in the same trial was Jim Guy Tucker, who succeeded Clinton as Governor of Arkansas.
